topic: What if you stood on the Moon and looked back at Earth?
notes: Planned on 2026-11-09 because the nightly run renders it in the night of 15→16, before the next Monday plan. Uses the top space backlog idea 'Why does the Moon always show us the same face?' (score 8) as a grounded what_if: premise (you land on the near side) → first hour (Earth hangs almost still in the sky, it never rises or sets; it only wobbles a little, libration) → first day (one lunar day lasts ~29.5 Earth days; the Sun takes about two weeks to cross the sky; Earth shows phases, opposite to the Moon's phases seen from Earth) → long term (the Moon drifts ~3.8 cm a year away) → what it teaches: the Moon is tidally locked, it turns once per orbit, so we always see the same face. Not scary: no dangers, no emergencies. Say 'astronomers' / 'NASA'. Sources to check: NASA (tidal locking, Moon facts), Live Science 'Earth phases from the Moon', Astronomy.com (Dec 2025) 'Why does the same side of the Moon always face Earth?', timeanddate (far side). Earth sprite: earth_tunnel_items:earth (phases masked in code). Category space: rotation after body. Format what_if: fewest reels in the log once 11/11 (quiz) and 11/13 (versus) are out. Remove the backlog line in topics.md when used.

topic: Myth or fact: does charging your phone overnight ruin the battery?
notes: Verdict stamp HALF TRUE (mostly myth): modern phones stop charging at 100% and some (iPhone Optimized Battery Charging, Pixel Adaptive Charging, Samsung Protect Battery) hold at ~80% overnight; what really ages a lithium-ion battery is heat and long hours at full charge, not the night itself. Where the belief comes from: older nickel batteries (NiCd/NiMH) had the 'memory effect' and cheap old chargers could overcharge. Evidence steps: 1) the phone's charge controller cuts the current at 100%; 2) heat (phone under a pillow, in a hot car; Apple says avoid above 35 C) and sitting at 100% are the real wear. Sources to check on the day: Apple support 'About Optimized Battery Charging' and apple.com/batteries/maximizing-performance, Battery University BU-808 and BU-807, Google Pixel Help 'Adaptive Charging', Samsung. Plausibility 16/11: many explainers agree (SlashGear, Mental Floss). No brand logos on the phones. Hook (control, question): 'Does charging overnight kill your battery?' First second: phone on a nightstand plugged in, battery icon draining/filling. Category tech: rotation after space (16/11). Format myth: tie at 2 reels with quiz/versus/what_if, used longest ago (8/11); myth also has the best skip rates so far (insights 16/11). Closing: not callback (16/11) nor cat_take (13/11); 'ask' fits here ('Do you charge overnight?') and was last used 8/11.

topic: Pop quiz: which of these was NOT at the first Thanksgiving in 1621?
notes: Themed reel for Thanksgiving (US) 26/11: 21/11 is the first publishing day inside the 7-day window and the event has 1 reel. Options: A) deer (venison), B) wild fowl, C) pumpkin pie. Answer C: Edward Winslow's 1621 letter (Mourt's Relation) mentions fowling and five deer brought by Massasoit's men (about 90 Wampanoag); the colonists had no butter or wheat flour and no ovens for pies, and sugar was scarce. Turkey itself is uncertain (Bradford mentions wild turkeys that autumn), so it is NOT an option. Say 'historians think', 'probably' where the sources do. Show the Wampanoag respectfully and accurately (17th-century New England, deerskin clothing; no Plains feather headdress); no 'Indians and pilgrims' cliches. Sources to check: Smithsonian Magazine 'What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving?', Plimoth Patuxet Museums, History.com, Mourt's Relation text. Plausibility 16/11: Smithsonian, Mental Floss, Wayne State all agree. Category history (themed reels may use any category; rotation resumes after tech). Format quiz (themed reels may use any format; not myth twice in a row). Length standard (control).

topic: Lightning vs the Sun: which is really hotter?
notes: 3 rounds, same units on both sides (degrees F or C, seconds): 1) surface heat: a lightning channel can reach ~50,000 F (NWS) vs the Sun's visible surface ~10,000 F (NASA) -> lightning, about 5x hotter; 2) how long: a flash lasts a fraction of a second vs the Sun shining for ~4.6 billion years -> Sun; 3) hottest point: lightning ~50,000 F vs the Sun's core ~27 million F -> Sun. Twist: the bolt beats the Sun's skin, but not its heart. Final 2-1 Sun. Fulgurite (sand fused to glass) as the visual proof of lightning heat. Sources to check: weather.gov/safety/lightning-temperature, NOAA SciJinks, NASA Sun facts (surface and core), Britannica. Plausibility 16/11: NWS and NASA give these figures. Hook (control, question): 'Lightning vs the Sun: which is hotter?' First second: a bolt flashing next to the Sun. Category science: rotation after tech (18/11; themed 21/11 does not count). Format versus: fewest reels once 18/11 (myth) and 21/11 (quiz) are out, tie with what_if, used longest ago (13/11).
